title: Supreme Court Clears Reopening of Tax Probe Against Former CJI's Sons
excerpt: Justices Pardiwala and Chandran dismissed Chetan and Nitin Sabharwal's appeals on October 28, upholding 2015 reassessment notices over Rs 255 crore share sales and a Delhi property purchase.
body:
• The Supreme Court on October 28 dismissed four appeals by Chetan and Nitin Sabharwal, sons of former Chief Justice of India Y. K. Sabharwal, upholding 2015 notices to reopen their income-tax assessments.
  • The case turns on October 2007 share sales totalling Rs 255 crore and the brothers' April 2010 purchase of a Delhi property, for which Section 54F relief was claimed.
  • The court held a post-assessment investigation report is tangible material for reopening, and that a Section 143(1) intimation is not an assessment — so no 'change of opinion' defence arises there.
  • The ruling lets reassessment proceed; it does not decide that any tax is actually payable.

The Supreme Court has cleared the way for the Income Tax Department to reopen assessments of businessmen Chetan and Nitin Sabharwal, sons of former Chief Justice of India Y. K. Sabharwal. In a judgment dated October 28, 2026, a bench of Justices J. B. Pardiwala and K. Vinod Chandran dismissed the brothers' four appeals and upheld reassessment notices issued on March 31, 2015.

The decision is about whether the department had a lawful basis to reopen the assessments for assessment years 2008-09 and 2009-10. It is not a finding that the brothers evaded tax, or that a particular amount is payable.

The Transactions Behind the Case

On October 19, 2007, Chetan Sabharwal, his brother and two other shareholders agreed to sell shares in Pawan Impex Pvt Ltd and SVIIT Software Pvt Ltd to GYS Real Estate Pvt Ltd, for consideration of Rs 195 crore and Rs 60 crore respectively — Rs 255 crore in total, with each seller entitled to a one-fourth share, according to Verdictum's report of the judgment.

https://x.com/iamrakeshbansal/status/2116728987720519890

Chetan Sabharwal filed his return for AY 2008-09 on September 25, 2008, declaring a loss of Rs 90.37 lakh. He later claimed relief under Section 54F of the Income Tax Act after buying a half share in a Delhi property in April 2010. His assessment under Section 143(3) was completed in December 2010.

An Investigation Unit report that reached the department after those assessments concluded the shares had been overvalued when measured against the cost of the companies' underlying land and buildings. The assessing officer issued a notice under Section 148 on March 31, 2015, and rejected the brothers' objections on September 24, 2015. The Delhi High Court dismissed their writ petition on August 6, 2019.

"The expression 'reason to believe' in Section 147 of the Act means cause or justification. The AO must have tangible material having a rational connection or a live link with the formation of the belief that income has escaped assessment, and need not have finally ascertained the fact by legal evidence or conclusion."

— Supreme Court bench of Justices J. B. Pardiwala and K. Vinod Chandran, as reported by Verdictum

What the Court Held

Reopening requires tangible material, not mere suspicion. The court held that an investigation report prepared after an assessment is fresh material on which an assessing officer can act, and that the sufficiency of the reasons is not justiciable at the notice stage — the only question is whether relevant material existed on which a reasonable person could form the belief that income had escaped assessment.

The brothers argued the reopening was a mere change of opinion, that overvaluation cannot cause escapement in a seller's hands, that the transactions had already been scrutinised, and that there was no failure to disclose. The court rejected the change-of-opinion argument on the facts. A change of opinion presupposes a conscious application of mind in the original assessment, the bench said. For Nitin Sabharwal, only a Section 143(1) intimation had issued — and an intimation is not an assessment, so no opinion had been formed. For Chetan Sabharwal, the court found the original assessment orders reflected no opinion on the specific matters raised in the notice.

The court also observed that escapement could take the form of a diversion of income, and that the recorded reasons covered the adjustment of gains to future years and the Section 54F claim, as summarised in analysis of the judgment in Chetan Sabharwal v. Assistant Commissioner of Income Tax (2026 INSC 1163).

What Happens Next

With the appeals dismissed, the 2015 notices stand and the reassessment proceedings can go ahead. The department can now examine the share valuations, the treatment of the gains, and the Section 54F claim through the reassessment process.

That process will decide liability — the Supreme Court judgment does not. For taxpayers and advisers more broadly, the ruling is a reminder that a silent or brief original assessment order may not establish that an issue was consciously decided, which is what a change-of-opinion challenge needs to succeed.
